questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design tenant-scoped upgrades, maintain isolation, and implement progressive release with concrete mechanisms.

## Key Concepts
- Kubernetes CRDs and multi-tenant mapping
- Canary rollouts and traffic splitting (Istio/Linkerd)
- Namespace-scoped isolation and rollback strategies
- Observability: SLIs for upgrade safety

## Code Example
```yaml
# Tenant CRD (simplified)
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: tenants.cnf.example.com
spec:
  group: cnf.example.com
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              tenantID: { type: string }
              namespace: { type: string }
              desiredVersion: { type: string }
  scope: Cluster
  names:
    plural: tenants
    singular: tenant
    kind: Tenant
    shortNames: [ tns ]
```

```yaml
# Tenant canary Deployment (tenant-a)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cnf-gateway
        tenant: tenant-a
        version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: gateway
        image: registry.example/cnf/gateway:v2
```

```yaml
# Istio TrafficSplit example for canary (tenant-a)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: cnf-gateway.tenant-a.svc.cluster.local
        subset: v1
      weight: 90
    - destination:
        host: cnf-gateway.tenant-a.svc.cluster.local
        subset: v2
      weight: 10
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you detect cross-tenant leakage during canary?  
- What metrics and alerting would you implement to enforce SLOs during rollout?

## Why This Is Asked
Assesses per-tenant authorization using a lightweight policy engine with ConfigMap-driven configuration. Emphasizes `X-TENANT-ID` header handling, status exposure, and end-to-end validation. Keeps the implementation approachable for beginners while demonstrating proper boundary isolation between tenants.

## Key Concepts
- Tenancy isolation
- Sidecar-based request authorization
- Kubernetes ConfigMaps as a policy store
- Path and method matching
- Health and status endpoints

## Code Example
```javascript
// Policy format loaded from ConfigMap
{
  "tenantA": { "/api/v1/*": ["GET", "POST"], "allow": true },
  "tenantB": { "/api/v2/*": ["GET"], "allow": true }
}
```

**YAML Manifest (cnf-gateway-namespace.yaml)**:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cnf-acl-policy
  namespace: cnf-gateway
data:
  cnf.acl.enabled: "true"
  cnf.acl.policy: |
    {
      "tenantA": {
        "/api/v1/*": ["GET", "POST"],
        "allow": true
      }
    }
```

- Sidecar pattern for tenant isolation
- Redis-based rate limiting with sliding window TTL and 429 responses

## Code Example
```go
func allow(tenant, path string) bool {
  key := tenant + ":" + pathHash(path)
  count, _ := redis.Incr(key).Result()
  if count == 1 { redis.Expire(key, time.Minute) }
  return count <= 100
}
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical policy design at the intersection of CNF gateways, Kubernetes admission control, and SBOM-driven security. It requires translating per-tenant risk tolerances into enforceable constraints and verifying end-to-end behavior.

## Key Concepts
- Gatekeeper/OPA integration for admission control
- Per-namespace configuration and binding
- SBOM-driven vulnerability data (CVSS) attached to images
- Rego-based enforcement logic and concise ConstraintTemplates
- End-to-end testing: apply templates, constraints, and verify allow/deny outcomes

## Code Example
```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate: CNFImageVuln
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: cnfimagevuln
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: CNFImageVuln
      scope: Cluster
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package cnfimagevuln
      violation[{"msg": msg}]
      # image.vulns is a list of {cve, cvss}
      violation[{"msg": msg}]
      {
        input.review.object.kind == "Deployment";
        ns := input.review.object.metadata.namespace;
        threshold := data.namespaceThresholds[ns];
        some i;
        vul := input.review.object.metadata.annotations["image.vulns"];
        cvss := vul[i].cvss;
        cvss > threshold; msg := sprintf("CVSS %v exceeds threshold %v for namespace %s", [cvss, threshold, ns]);
      }
```
```yaml
# Constraint: Bind per-namespace threshold
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: CNFImageVuln
metadata:
  name: cnf-image-vuln-namespace
spec:
  namespaceSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - {key: "cnf.namespace", operator: In, values: ["default"]}
```
```yaml
# Test manifest: should fail for CVSS > threshold and pass otherwise
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: test-cnf
  namespace: default
  annotations:
    image.vulns: "[{\"cve\":\"CVE-2024-0001\",\"cvss\":9}]"
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test-cnf
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test-cnf
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: example/cnf:latest
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle multi-tenant overrides for temporary risk surges?
- How would you test performance impact of SBOM parsing in high-scale deployments?
